rows: Access tokens expire after one week and there is no refresh token.
The token identifies the user by username, not by user id.
The Authorization header must use the prefix Token, not Bearer.
Bad tokens, wrong prefixes and unknown users are answered with 403, not 401.
Login returns the same error for an unknown email and a wrong password.
Passwords are hashed with bcrypt through a passlib CryptContext.
A separately stored per-user salt is prepended to the password before hashing.
An article slug is derived from its title with slugify.
Updating an article title regenerates its slug, so its URL changes.
Only the author may update or delete an article, checked by comparing usernames.
Deleting a user keeps their articles and sets author_id to NULL.
updated_at is maintained by a Postgres trigger, not by application code.
Database access uses raw SQL files loaded with aiosql on asyncpg, not an ORM.
Article lists default to 20 items and have no upper limit.
API models use camelCase JSON aliases generated from snake_case field names.
Datetimes are serialized as UTC ISO strings ending in Z.
Access tokens are signed with the HS256 algorithm using one shared secret key.
Access tokens are signed with the symmetric HS256 algorithm.
Every access token carries the fixed subject claim access.
Each user gets a random salt created with bcrypt.gensalt.
Request validation failures return HTTP 422 with an errors list of the validator's error objects.
Registering with a username or email that is already taken is answered with HTTP 400.
Only an article's author, matched by username, may modify the article.
Cross-origin calls are allowed from the origins in allowed_hosts, which default to every origin.
CORS allows every origin by default, with credentials allowed.
The database pool is fixed at 10 connections through min_connection_count and max_connection_count.
Creating a tag that already exists is ignored by the insert statement.
